media.title: Non-intersecting, secant, tangent - 90-second overview
media.description: A 90-second animated explainer. A straight line sweeps across a circle in three stages: far above (non-intersecting), cutting through (secant), and finally grazing at a single point (tangent). Each stage is held on screen with an on-screen label identifying the line type and the number of common points.

Pause at 30s (attempt-before-reveal) and ask 'What do you think the line would become if it moved right through the circle?' and again at 50s: 'What happens at the exact boundary between cutting through and missing entirely?' After the video, ask the student to list the three cases and count the common points in each.

Scene 2 (10-30s): a straight Navy Blue line labelled 'PQ' enters from the left, high above the circle, sharing zero points; a caption fades in reading 'non-intersecting line - 0 common points'. content.text:
So, let us consider a circle and a line PQ. There can be three possibilities given in the figure below:

In (i), the line PQ and the circle have no common point. In this case, PQ is called a non-intersecting line with respect to the circle. In (ii), there are two common points A and B that the line PQ and the circle have. In this case, we call the line PQ a secant of the circle. In (iii), there is only one point A which is common to the line PQ and the circle. In this case, the line is called a tangent to the circle.

You might have seen a pulley fitted over a well which is used in taking out water from the well. Here the rope on both sides of the pulley, if considered as a ray, is like a tangent to the circle representing the pulley.

Is there any position of the line with respect to the circle other than the types given above? You can see that there cannot be any other type of position of the line with respect to the circle. In this chapter, we will study about the existence of the tangents to a circle and also study some of their properties.

content.text:
Earlier, you have seen that a tangent to a circle is a line that intersects the circle at only one point.

To understand the existence of the tangent to a circle at a point, let us perform the following activities:

Activity : Take a circular wire and attach a straight wire AB at a point P of the circular wire so that it can rotate about the point P in a plane. Put the system on a table and gently rotate the wire AB about the point P to get different positions of the straight wire.

In various positions, the wire intersects the circular wire at P and at another point Q₁ or Q₂ or Q₃, etc. In one position, you will see that it will intersect the circle at the point P only (see position A′B′ of AB). This shows that a tangent exists at the point P of the circle. On rotating further, you can observe that in all other positions of AB, it will intersect the circle at P and at another point, say R₁ or R₂ or R₃, etc. So, you can observe that there is only one tangent at a point of the circle.

While doing activity above, you must have observed that as the position AB moves towards the position A′B′, the common point, say Q₁, of the line AB and the circle gradually comes nearer and nearer to the common point P. Ultimately, it coincides with the point P in the position A′B′ of AB. Again note, what happens if 'AB' is rotated rightwards about P? The common point R₃ gradually comes nearer and nearer to P and ultimately coincides with P. So, what we see is:

The tangent to a circle is a special case of the secant, when the two end points of its corresponding chord coincide.

content.text:
Activity : On a paper, draw a circle and a secant PQ of the circle. Draw various lines parallel to the secant on both sides of it. You will find that after some steps, the length of the chord cut by the lines will gradually decrease, i.e., the two points of intersection of the line and the circle are coming closer and closer. In one case, it becomes zero on one side of the secant and in another case, it becomes zero on the other side of the secant. See the positions P′Q′ and P″Q″ of the secant in the figure. These are the tangents to the circle parallel to the given secant PQ. This also helps you to see that there cannot be more than two tangents parallel to a given secant.

This activity also establishes, what you must have observed, while doing the first activity, namely, a tangent is the secant when both of the end points of the corresponding chord coincide.

The common point of the tangent and the circle is called the point of contact [the point A in the first figure (iii)] and the tangent is said to touch the circle at the common point.

content.text:
Proof : We are given a circle with centre O and a tangent XY to the circle at a point P. We need to prove that OP is perpendicular to XY.

Take a point Q on XY other than P and join OQ.

The point Q must lie outside the circle. (Why? Note that if Q lies inside the circle, XY will become a secant and not a tangent to the circle). Therefore, OQ is longer than the radius OP of the circle. That is,
OQ > OP.

Since this happens for every point on the line XY except the point P, OP is the shortest of all the distances of the point O to the points of XY. So OP is perpendicular to XY (as you know, the shortest distance from a point to a line is the perpendicular one).

content.text:
To get an idea of the number of tangents from a point on a circle, let us perform the following activity:

Activity : Draw a circle on a paper. Take a point P inside it. Can you draw a tangent to the circle through this point? You will find that all the lines through this point intersect the circle in two points. So, it is not possible to draw any tangent to a circle through a point inside it.

Next take a point P on the circle and draw tangents through this point. You have already observed that there is only one tangent to the circle at such a point.

Finally, take a point P outside the circle and try to draw tangents to the circle from this point. What do you observe? You will find that you can draw exactly two tangents to the circle through this point.

We can summarise these facts as follows:
Case 1 : There is no tangent to a circle passing through a point lying inside the circle.
Case 2 : There is one and only one tangent to a circle passing through a point lying on the circle.
Case 3 : There are exactly two tangents to a circle through a point lying outside the circle.

In (iii), T₁ and T₂ are the points of contact of the tangents PT₁ and PT₂ respectively.

The length of the segment of the tangent from the external point P and the point of contact with the circle is called the length of the tangent from the point P to the circle.

concepts.concept_name: The equal-tangents theorem: try it first

content.text:
Proof : We are given a circle with centre O, a point P lying outside the circle and two tangents PQ, PR on the circle from P. We are required to prove that PQ = PR.

For this, we join OP, OQ and OR. Then ∠OQP and ∠ORP are right angles, because these are angles between the radii and tangents, and according to the tangent-radius theorem they are right angles. Now in right triangles OQP and ORP,
OQ = OR (Radii of the same circle)
OP = OP (Common)
Therefore, ∆OQP ≅ ∆ORP (RHS)
This gives PQ = PR (CPCT)

1. The theorem can also be proved by using the Pythagoras Theorem as follows:
PQ² = OP² − OQ² = OP² − OR² = PR² (As OQ = OR)
which gives PQ = PR.
2. Note also that ∠OPQ = ∠OPR. Therefore, OP is the angle bisector of ∠QPR, i.e., the centre lies on the bisector of the angle between the two tangents.

content.text: Prove that in two concentric circles, the chord of the larger circle, which touches the smaller circle, is bisected at the point of contact.
content.question: Prove that in two concentric circles, the chord of the larger circle, which touches the smaller circle, is bisected at the point of contact.
content.publication_text: Prove that in two concentric circles, the chord of the larger circle, which touches the smaller circle, is bisected at the point of contact.

content.text:
We are given two concentric circles C₁ and C₂ with centre O and a chord AB of the larger circle C₁ which touches the smaller circle C₂ at the point P. We need to prove that AP = BP.

Let us join OP. Then, AB is a tangent to C₂ at P and OP is its radius. Therefore, by the tangent-radius theorem,
OP ⊥ AB

Now AB is a chord of the circle C₁ and OP ⊥ AB. Therefore, OP is the bisector of the chord AB, as the perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord,
i.e., AP = BP

content.text: Two tangents TP and TQ are drawn to a circle with centre O from an external point T. Prove that ∠PTQ = 2 ∠OPQ.
content.question: Two tangents TP and TQ are drawn to a circle with centre O from an external point T. Prove that ∠PTQ = 2 ∠OPQ.
content.publication_text: Two tangents TP and TQ are drawn to a circle with centre O from an external point T. Prove that ∠PTQ = 2 ∠OPQ.

content.text:
We are given a circle with centre O, an external point T and two tangents TP and TQ to the circle, where P, Q are the points of contact. We need to prove that
∠PTQ = 2 ∠OPQ
Let ∠PTQ = θ
Now, by the equal-tangents theorem, TP = TQ. So, TPQ is an isosceles triangle.
Therefore, ∠TPQ = ∠TQP = ½(180° − θ) = 90° − ½θ
Also, by the tangent-radius theorem, ∠OPT = 90°
So, ∠OPQ = ∠OPT − ∠TPQ = 90° − (90° − ½θ) = ½θ = ½ ∠PTQ
This gives ∠PTQ = 2 ∠OPQ

content.text: PQ is a chord of length 8 cm of a circle of radius 5 cm. The tangents at P and Q intersect at a point T. Find the length TP.
content.question: PQ is a chord of length 8 cm of a circle of radius 5 cm. The tangents at P and Q intersect at a point T. Find the length TP.
content.publication_text: PQ is a chord of length 8 cm of a circle of radius 5 cm. The tangents at P and Q intersect at a point T. Find the length TP.

content.text:
Join OT. Let it intersect PQ at the point R. Then ∆TPQ is isosceles and TO is the angle bisector of ∠PTQ. So, OT ⊥ PQ and therefore, OT bisects PQ which gives PR = RQ = 4 cm.
Also, OR = √(OP² − PR²) = √(5² − 4²) cm = 3 cm.
Now, ∠TPR + ∠RPO = 90° = ∠TPR + ∠PTR (Why?)
So, ∠RPO = ∠PTR
Therefore, right triangle TRP is similar to the right triangle PRO by AA similarity.
This gives TP / PO = RP / RO, i.e., TP / 5 = 4 / 3 or TP = 20/3 cm.

Note. TP can also be found by using the Pythagoras Theorem, as follows:
Let TP = x and TR = y. Then
x² = y² + 16 (Taking right ∆PRT)    (1)
x² + 5² = (y + 3)² (Taking right ∆OPT)    (2)
Subtracting (1) from (2), we get
25 = 6y − 7 or y = 32/6 = 16/3
Therefore, x² = (16/3)² + 16 = 16(16/9 + 1) = 16(16 + 9)/9 = 16 · 25/9    [From (1)]
or x = 20/3

concepts.concept_name: How long is the tangent from where two tangents meet?

content.text:
Q. In the tangent-length example, why is ∠TPR + ∠RPO = 90° = ∠TPR + ∠PTR?
A. ∠TPR + ∠RPO is the whole angle ∠TPO between the tangent TP and the radius OP, and a tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact, so it is 90°. In the right triangle TRP the right angle is at R, so the other two angles, ∠TPR and ∠PTR, add up to 180° − 90° = 90°.

HOOK: Look at any moving bicycle on a Delhi street. Its round wheel meets the flat road at exactly one point at every instant. The road is not cutting through the wheel, and it is not missing the wheel either - it is touching it in a very specific way. In this chapter we will study that special kind of touching, which geometers call tangency.

RECALL: From Class IX you already know a circle as the set of all points in a plane at a constant distance (the radius) from a fixed point (the centre). You also met terms like chord, segment, sector, and arc. Now we turn our attention to what happens when a straight line and a circle share the same plane.

CORE: Consider any circle and any straight line PQ drawn in its plane. Only three possibilities arise, shown in Fig. 10.1.

  (i) The line PQ has no common point with the circle. We call PQ a non-intersecting line with respect to the circle.

  (ii) The line PQ meets the circle at two distinct points, A and B. Here PQ is called a secant of the circle.

  (iii) The line PQ meets the circle at exactly one point, A. In this case the line is called a tangent to the circle.

There is no fourth case, because a straight line and a circle can share zero, one, or two common points - never three.

WORKED WALK-THROUGH (bicycle wheel on the road): Recall the cycle on the street. The wheel is the circle, the road is the line. Since the road shares only the single contact point underneath the axle, the road is a tangent to the wheel - case (iii). If the road were instead a flat plank pressed right through the wheel (an accident!), it would cross the circle at two points and become a secant. A ceiling far above the cycle, sharing no point with the wheel, is a non-intersecting line.

WORKED WALK-THROUGH - second scenario (well pulley in a village): Picture a pulley fitted over a well used to lift buckets of water in rural Rajasthan. The rope on either side of the pulley, if extended as a straight ray, just grazes the pulley at one point. Each of those two rays is a tangent to the circular pulley wheel, as you can see in Fig. 10.2.

WHY THIS STEP? Why not say the rope is a secant? Because the rope does not pass through the pulley body. It meets the circle only where it rests on the rim - a single point of contact - which matches the definition of a tangent.

ERROR ALERT: A common mistake is to confuse a tangent with a chord. A chord joins two points ON the circle and lies INSIDE; a tangent touches the circle at one point and extends AWAY from it on both sides. Another confusion is between secant and tangent - remember, a secant cuts through (two common points) and a tangent only touches (one common point).

Is there any position of the line with respect to the circle other than these three? No - you can verify for yourself that only these three exist. In this chapter, we will now study the existence of tangents to a circle and some of their properties.

HOOK: We already have the name ‘tangent’ from the previous topic. But where does a tangent actually come from? Is it a completely new object, or does it emerge naturally from something we already know - a secant? We will investigate through two hands-on activities.

RECALL: From topic 1 we know: a tangent* to a circle is a line that intersects the circle at only one point. We also know that a secant intersects the circle at two points. Keep these two pictures in mind as we experiment.

CORE: Imagine that a secant PQ can be tilted or slid until its two intersection points with the circle come closer and closer together. What do you expect to happen when they finally meet? We are about to see, first by rotation (Activity 1) and then by parallel sliding (Activity 2).

Activity 1 - Rotating wire: Take a circular wire and attach a straight wire AB at a point P of the circular wire so that AB can rotate freely about the point P in a plane. Put the system on a table and gently rotate the wire AB about the point P to get different positions of the straight wire, as shown in Fig. 10.3 (i).

OBSERVE: In most positions, the wire crosses the circular wire at P and at a second point - call it Q1, or Q2, or Q3, depending on the angle. But in one special position, the wire intersects the circle at the point P only. Let us name this position A′B′ of AB. This is the tangent at P.

WHY THIS STEP? Why is only one position a tangent, while all nearby positions are secants? Because rotating even slightly brings a second intersection point back - either R1, R2, or R3 on the other side. The tangent is the unique knife-edge position between secants on either side.

While doing Activity 1, you must have observed that as the position AB moves towards the position A′B′, the common point Q1 gradually comes nearer and nearer to the common point P. Ultimately Q1 coincides with P in the position A′B′ of AB. If AB is rotated rightwards about P, the common point R3 also gradually approaches P and ultimately coincides with P. So we see:

  The tangent to a circle is a special case of the secant, when the two end points of its corresponding chord coincide.

*The word ‘tangent’ comes from the Latin word ‘tangere’, which means to touch, and was introduced by the Danish mathematician Thomas Fineke in 1583.

Activity 2 - Parallel sliding: On a paper, draw a circle and a secant PQ of the circle. Draw various lines parallel to the secant on both sides of it. You will find that after some steps, the length of the chord cut by the lines will gradually decrease - the two points of intersection of the line and the circle are coming closer and closer, as shown in Fig. 10.3 (ii). In one case the chord length becomes zero on one side of the secant, and in another case it becomes zero on the other side of the secant. Call these two limiting lines P′Q′ and P″Q″ in Fig. 10.3 (ii). These are the tangents to the circle parallel to the given secant PQ. This also shows that there cannot be more than two tangents parallel to a given secant.

This activity establishes, once again, the same truth you saw in Activity 1: a tangent is the secant when both endpoints of the corresponding chord coincide.

The common point of the tangent and the circle is called the point of contact (the point A in Fig. 10.1 (iii)), and the tangent is said to touch the circle at the common point.

APPLICATION - wheel on the ground: Now look around you. Have you seen a bicycle or a bullock-cart moving on a road? Look at its wheels. All the spokes of a wheel are along its radii. Note the position of the wheel with respect to its movement on the ground - do you see a tangent anywhere? See Fig. 10.4. In fact, the wheel rolls along a line which is a tangent to the circle representing the wheel. Notice also that in every position, the radius through the point of contact with the ground appears to be at right angles to the tangent (see Fig. 10.4). That right-angle observation is the key property we will now prove in the next topic.

ERROR ALERT: Many students mistakenly believe that a tangent can somehow ‘slightly cross’ the circle, as if it grazes through a tiny segment. It does not. A tangent and a circle share exactly one point - no more, no less. The limiting argument (secant’s two intersection points merging into one) is a precise mathematical operation, not a physical slight overlap.

10.2 Tangent to a Circle

In the previous section, you have seen that a tangent* to a circle is a line that intersects the circle at only one point.

To understand the existence of the tangent to a circle at a point, let us perform the following activities:

Activity 1 : Take a circular wire and attach a straight wire AB at a point P of the circular wire so that it can rotate about the point P in a plane. Put the system on a table and gently rotate the wire AB about the point P to get different positions of the straight wire [see Fig. 10.3(i)].

In various positions, the wire intersects the circular wire at P and at another point Q1 or Q2 or Q3, etc. In one position, you will see that it will intersect the circle at the point P only (see position A′B′ of AB). This shows that a tangent exists at the point P of the circle. On rotating further, you can observe that in all other positions of AB, it will intersect the circle at P and at another point, say R1 or R2 or R3, etc. So, you can observe that there is only one tangent at a point of the circle.

While doing activity above, you must have observed that as the position AB moves towards the position A′B′, the common point, say Q1, of the line AB and the circle gradually comes nearer and nearer to the common point P. Ultimately, it coincides with the point P in the position A′B′ of AB. Again note, what happens if 'AB' is rotated rightwards about P? The common point R3 gradually comes nearer and nearer to P and ultimately coincides with P. So, what we see is:

The tangent to a circle is a special case of the secant, when the two end points of its corresponding chord coincide.

*The word 'tangent' comes from the Latin word 'tangere', which means to touch and was introduced by the Danish mathematician Thomas Fineke in 1583.

Activity 2 : On a paper, draw a circle and a secant PQ of the circle. Draw various lines parallel to the secant on both sides of it. You will find that after some steps, the length of the chord cut by the lines will gradually decrease, i.e., the two points of intersection of the line and the circle are coming closer and closer [see Fig. 10.3(ii)]. In one case, it becomes zero on one side of the secant and in another case, it becomes zero on the other side of the secant. See the positions P′Q′ and P″Q″ of the secant in Fig. 10.3 (ii). These are the tangents to the circle parallel to the given secant PQ. This also helps you to see that there cannot be more than two tangents parallel to a given secant.

This activity also establishes, what you must have observed, while doing Activity 1, namely, a tangent is the secant when both of the end points of the corresponding chord coincide.

The common point of the tangent and the circle is called the point of contact [the point A in Fig. 10.1 (iii)] and the tangent is said to touch the circle at the common point.

Now look around you. Have you seen a bicycle or a cart moving? Look at its wheels. All the spokes of a wheel are along its radii. Now note the position of the wheel with respect to its movement on the ground. Do you see any tangent anywhere? (See Fig. 10.4). In fact, the wheel moves along a line which is a tangent to the circle representing the wheel. Also, notice that in all positions, the radius through the point of contact with the ground appears to be at right angles to the tangent (see Fig. 10.4). We shall now prove this property of the tangent.

carried_over_topics.summary: The topic proves Theorem 10.1: the tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact. Given a circle with centre O and tangent XY at point P, pick any point Q on XY other than P. Because XY is a tangent, Q must lie outside the circle, so OQ > OP. This inequality holds for every Q ≠ P, so OP is the shortest distance from O to XY. Since the shortest distance from a point to a line is perpendicular, OP ⊥ XY. The theorem implies only one tangent exists at any point of a circle, and the radius through the contact point is sometimes called the normal.
carried_over_topics.topic_name: Theorem 10.1 - The Tangent at Any Point of a Circle is Perpendicular to the Radius Through the Point of Contact

carried_over_topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: In the last topic we noticed something visually striking about a rolling wheel: the spoke that meets the ground seems to be perpendicular to the ground. That was a rough observation from a figure. Can we turn it into a proof? Yes - and the proof uses nothing more than a distance argument.

RECALL: From topic 2 we know that a tangent touches the circle at exactly one point, called the point of contact. From earlier chapters you also know that a radius is the segment from the centre to any point on the circle, and all radii of the same circle have the same length.

CORE - We are about to prove our first property of tangents.

THEOREM STATEMENT:
  Theorem 10.1: The tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact.

GIVEN:
  A circle with centre O, and a tangent XY to the circle at a point P.

TO PROVE:
  OP is perpendicular to XY, i.e., OP ⊥ XY.

CONSTRUCTION:
  Take any point Q on XY other than P, and join OQ (see Fig. 10.5).

PROOF STEPS:

  (i) The point Q must lie outside the circle.
      WHY? Because if Q were inside the circle, the line XY would enter the circle's interior and exit again - making it a secant, with two common points, not a tangent with only one. That contradicts the fact that XY is a tangent.

  (ii) Since Q lies outside the circle, its distance from the centre is greater than the radius. In symbols:
         OQ > OP.
      WHY? Because any point outside a circle is at a distance greater than the radius, by the definition of ‘outside’. OP, however, is exactly a radius, because P lies on the circle.

  (iii) The inequality OQ > OP holds for every point Q on the line XY except for the point P itself.
      WHY? Step (i) applied to any Q on XY other than P showed Q must be outside the circle. Only the single contact point P is on the circle; everyone else on XY is outside.

  (iv) Therefore, OP is the shortest of all the distances from the centre O to the points of the line XY.
      WHY? If every other distance OQ is strictly greater than OP, then OP is the smallest (minimum) such distance.

  (v) The shortest distance from a point to a line is the perpendicular distance (as shown in Theorem A1.7 of the Class IX appendix). So OP must be perpendicular to XY.

CONCLUSION:
  Hence, OP ⊥ XY. The tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact.  □

REMARKS:

  1. A direct consequence of this theorem is: at any point on a circle there can be one and only one tangent. (If two different tangents existed at P, both would have to be perpendicular to OP at P - but only one line through P is perpendicular to OP, so the two tangents must coincide.)

  2. The line containing the radius through the point of contact is also sometimes called the normal to the circle at the point.

ERROR ALERT: A common misconception is that the perpendicularity proof needs trigonometry or a construction of extra triangles. It does not. The entire logic rests on one idea - the shortest distance from a point to a line is perpendicular. The hard part is establishing, via step (i), that every point of XY except P lies outside the circle.

WHY THIS STEP? (reflective): Why did we avoid drawing any extra triangle or angle? Because the theorem is most cleanly seen as a statement about distances: the contact point minimises the distance from the centre, and the minimising direction from a point to a line is always the perpendicular.

HOOK: From a random point of your choosing, how many tangents can you draw to a given circle? Is the answer always two? Always one? Or does it depend on where you stand relative to the circle?

RECALL: We already know (from Theorem 10.1) that at any point of a circle there is exactly one tangent - the line through that point perpendicular to the radius there. What happens when our chosen point is NOT on the circle - when it lies strictly inside, or strictly outside?

CORE: To answer this, let us do one more activity.

Activity 3 - Three positions of a point:

  Step 1. Draw a circle on a paper. Take a point P inside it. Try to draw a tangent to the circle through this point. What happens? You will find that every line you can draw through P cuts the circle at two points - it is always a secant. So it is not possible to draw any tangent to a circle through a point inside it. See Fig. 10.6 (i).

  Step 2. Next, take a point P on the circle and try to draw tangents through this point. From topic 3 you already know the answer: there is only one tangent through a point of the circle. See Fig. 10.6 (ii).

  Step 3. Finally, take a point P outside the circle and try to draw tangents to the circle from this point. What do you observe? With a ruler you will find that you can draw exactly two tangents to the circle through this point. See Fig. 10.6 (iii).

We can summarise these facts as the three cases for the number of tangents from a point:

  Case 1: There is no tangent to a circle passing through a point lying inside the circle.

  Case 2: There is one and only one tangent to a circle passing through a point lying on the circle.

  Case 3: There are exactly two tangents to a circle through a point lying outside the circle.

In Fig. 10.6 (iii), T1 and T2 are the points of contact of the two tangents PT1 and PT2 respectively.

DEFINITION - Length of a tangent:
  The length of the segment of the tangent from the external point P to the point of contact with the circle is called the length of the tangent from the point P to the circle. So in Fig. 10.6 (iii), PT1 and PT2 are the lengths of the two tangents from P.

WORKED WALK-THROUGH (kabaddi raider outside a circular mat):
Picture a round kabaddi mat drawn on a school ground in Pune. A raider stands one metre outside the mat. From that position, how many straight paths can the raider aim that just touch the mat at a single point and miss the rest of it? Exactly two - one on each side of the mat. That matches Case 3: a point outside the circle yields two tangents. If the raider steps onto the mat's edge, there is exactly one such path (Case 2). If the raider stands inside the mat, there is none (Case 1).

WHY THIS STEP? Why does a point inside allow ZERO tangents? Because every line through an interior point must exit the circle on both sides, hitting the boundary twice - two common points, which makes every such line a secant, not a tangent.

OBSERVATION - two tangent lengths from a single external point:
In Fig. 10.6 (iii), the lengths PT1 and PT2 have a common property. Can you find this? Measure PT1 and PT2 - are these equal? In fact, this is always so. We will give a proof of this fact in the next topic.

ERROR ALERT: A student sometimes thinks that from a point very far outside the circle, more than two tangents are possible - perhaps three or four, because the point is ‘so far away’. This is wrong. Distance does not add more tangents. The count is determined by the point's POSITION (inside / on / outside), not by how far outside. Outside always means exactly two.

carried_over_topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: At the end of the last topic we noticed that the two tangents drawn from an external point to a circle seemed to be equal in length. That was a hunch from a measurement. Is it always true? Let us prove it rigorously.

RECALL: From topic 3 (Theorem 10.1) we know that a tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact. From earlier chapters we know the RHS congruence rule: two right triangles are congruent if the hypotenuse and one side are respectively equal. We will combine these two facts.

CORE - The second tangent theorem.

THEOREM STATEMENT:
  Theorem 10.2: The lengths of tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal.

GIVEN:
  A circle with centre O, a point P lying outside the circle, and two tangents PQ and PR from P to the circle (see Fig. 10.7).

TO PROVE:
  PQ = PR.

CONSTRUCTION:
  Join OP, OQ, and OR.

PROOF STEPS:

  (i) ∠OQP = 90° and ∠ORP = 90°.
      WHY? OQ is a radius and PQ is the tangent at Q, so by Theorem 10.1 the radius is perpendicular to the tangent at the point of contact. The same reasoning applies at R. Both angles are between the radii and the tangents.

  (ii) In right triangles OQP and ORP:
         OQ = OR    (Radii of the same circle)
         OP = OP    (Common hypotenuse)
      WHY? OQ and OR are both radii of the same circle, so they must be equal in length. The segment OP is shared by both triangles, so it is identical in each.

  (iii) Therefore, ∆OQP ≅ ∆ORP    (RHS congruence criterion)
      WHY? Each triangle is a right triangle (from step (i)); the hypotenuses are equal (both are OP); and one pair of sides is equal (OQ = OR). That matches the RHS rule exactly.

  (iv) Hence, PQ = PR    (CPCT - corresponding parts of congruent triangles)

CONCLUSION:
  The two tangent lengths from an external point P are equal: PQ = PR.  □

REMARKS:

  1. The theorem can also be proved using the Pythagoras Theorem:
       PQ² = OP² − OQ² = OP² − OR² = PR²    (because OQ = OR)
     which gives PQ = PR.

  2. Note also that ∠OPQ = ∠OPR (also a CPCT consequence). Therefore, OP is the angle bisector of ∠QPR - i.e., the centre lies on the bisector of the angle between the two tangents. This is a useful result we will meet again.

WHY THIS STEP? Why did we bother to join OQ, OR, and OP as a construction step? Because the proof relies on comparing two triangles, and those three segments are exactly the edges needed. Without the construction we would have a picture with no triangles to work with.

ERROR ALERT: A frequent mistake is to apply SAS or ASA here instead of RHS. The two tangents PQ and PR are not the given equal sides - that is what we are trying to prove! The congruence must use only the facts we already have: a right angle, a shared hypotenuse OP, and the equal radii OQ = OR. That combination is RHS, not SAS.

HOOK: In some geometric configurations, a chord of one circle lies inside another, smaller circle's neighbourhood. Could there be a clean, surprising relationship between the two? Here is a classic result that uses only Theorem 10.1 - no extra tools.

RECALL: Two circles sharing the same centre are called concentric. From Theorem 10.1 we know that a tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact. From earlier chapters we know a key chord fact: the perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord.

CORE - Worked Example 1 (concentric circles and a tangent chord):

THE PROBLEM (in words):
  Prove that in two concentric circles, the chord of the larger circle which touches the smaller circle is bisected at the point of contact.

WHAT'S THE SITUATION?:
  Two circles share the centre O. A straight line segment AB is drawn so that it is a chord of the larger circle C1 but is also tangent to the smaller circle C2, touching it at a single point P. See Fig. 10.8.

WHAT DO WE KNOW?:
  • O is the common centre of both circles.
  • AB is a chord of C1 (so A and B lie on C1).
  • AB touches C2 at the single point P (so AB is a tangent to C2).
  • OP is a radius of C2.

WHAT DO WE WANT TO FIND?:
  We want to prove that P is the midpoint of AB - i.e., AP = BP.

SOLUTION:

  Step 1. Join OP. (Construction.)

  Step 2. Since AB is a tangent to C2 at P and OP is the radius of C2 at that point of contact,
            OP ⊥ AB    (by Theorem 10.1).

  Step 3. Now look at the larger circle C1. AB is a chord of C1, and OP is a segment from O (the centre of C1) perpendicular to AB. So OP is a perpendicular from the centre to the chord AB.

  Step 4. By a result you already know, the perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord. Therefore OP bisects AB at P.

  Step 5. Hence AP = BP.

CALLBACK - everyday image: Earlier we pictured two concentric rotis on a plate, cut by a single knife that just grazes the smaller roti. The point where the knife touches the smaller roti turns out to be the midpoint of the knife's contact across the larger roti. That is exactly this result.

WHY THIS STEP? Why did we have to join OP explicitly? Because the proof needs OP to play two roles at once: a radius of C2 (giving perpendicularity to the tangent AB) and a perpendicular from the centre of C1 to its chord AB (giving the bisection). Joining OP makes this dual role visible.

ERROR ALERT: Some students try to argue that AP = BP by symmetry alone (“The picture looks symmetric!”). Visual symmetry is not a proof. The proof must cite a theorem - here, that a perpendicular from the centre bisects any chord it meets.

HOOK: When two tangents are drawn from an external point to a circle, two angles immediately attract attention - the angle between the tangents themselves, and the angle between each tangent and the chord joining the two points of contact. Are these angles related? The answer is yes, and elegantly so.

RECALL: From Theorem 10.2 we know that the two tangents from an external point have equal lengths. From Theorem 10.1 we know that each tangent is perpendicular to the radius at its point of contact. We will combine both properties with the isosceles-triangle angle sum.

CORE - Worked Example 2 (angle between two tangents):

THE PROBLEM (in words):
  Two tangents TP and TQ are drawn to a circle with centre O from an external point T. Prove that ∠PTQ = 2 ∠OPQ.

WHAT'S THE SITUATION?:
  A circle has centre O. From a point T outside it, two tangents are drawn touching the circle at P and at Q. See Fig. 10.9.

WHAT DO WE KNOW?:
  • TP and TQ are tangents from T, so by Theorem 10.2, TP = TQ.
  • OP and OQ are radii at the two points of contact.
  • By Theorem 10.1, ∠OPT = 90° and ∠OQT = 90°.

WHAT DO WE WANT TO FIND?:
  A proof that the angle between the two tangents at T is exactly twice the angle ∠OPQ.

SOLUTION:

  Step 1. Let ∠PTQ = θ.    (We introduce θ as a convenient variable for the unknown angle.)

  Step 2. By Theorem 10.2, TP = TQ. So ∆TPQ is an isosceles triangle, with TP and TQ as the two equal sides and PQ as the base.

  Step 3. In an isosceles triangle, the base angles are equal. So
            ∠TPQ = ∠TQP.
          And the three angles of ∆TPQ sum to 180°:
            ∠TPQ + ∠TQP + ∠PTQ = 180°.
          Substituting ∠TPQ = ∠TQP and ∠PTQ = θ,
            2 · ∠TPQ + θ = 180°
            ∠TPQ = ½(180° − θ) = 90° − ½θ.

  Step 4. By Theorem 10.1, the radius OP is perpendicular to the tangent TP at P, so
            ∠OPT = 90°.

  Step 5. The angle ∠OPQ is the difference between ∠OPT and ∠TPQ (look at the figure at vertex P):
            ∠OPQ = ∠OPT − ∠TPQ = 90° − (90° − ½θ) = ½θ.

  Step 6. Therefore ∠OPQ = ½θ = ½ ∠PTQ, which gives
            ∠PTQ = 2 ∠OPQ.

CONCLUSION:
  Hence, ∠PTQ = 2 ∠OPQ.  □

WHY THIS STEP? Why did we let ∠PTQ = θ instead of working with the angle directly? Because naming the unknown θ lets us combine two angle facts (isosceles-triangle base angles and tangent-radius perpendicularity) into one clean algebraic line. Without the variable, the final equation ∠PTQ = 2 ∠OPQ would be harder to assemble.

ERROR ALERT: A common mistake is to confuse ∠OPQ with ∠OPT. These are different: ∠OPT is the full 90° angle between the radius OP and the tangent TP, while ∠OPQ is the angle between OP and the chord PQ inside that right angle. Reading the figure carefully is essential. The key identity is ∠OPT = ∠OPQ + ∠TPQ, which we rearranged in Step 5.

HOOK: Our third example brings together almost every tool we have built so far - Theorem 10.1, Theorem 10.2, similar triangles, and the Pythagoras Theorem. If you can follow this example, you have mastered the chapter's core techniques.

RECALL: We know from Theorem 10.2 that tangents from an external point are equal. From Theorem 10.1 each tangent is perpendicular to the radius at its point of contact. From earlier chapters we know that a perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord, the Pythagoras Theorem in a right triangle, and the AA similarity criterion.

CORE - Worked Example 3 (tangent length from an external point):

THE PROBLEM (in words):
  PQ is a chord of length 8 cm of a circle of radius 5 cm. The tangents at P and Q intersect at a point T (see Fig. 10.10). Find the length TP.

WHAT'S THE SITUATION?:
  A circle with centre O has radius 5 cm. Two points P and Q on the circle are joined by a chord of length 8 cm. Tangents are drawn to the circle at P and at Q. These two tangents meet at an external point T.

WHAT DO WE KNOW?:
  • OP = OQ = 5 cm (both are radii).
  • PQ = 8 cm (given chord length).
  • TP and TQ are tangents at P and Q; by Theorem 10.2, TP = TQ.
  • By Theorem 10.1, ∠OPT = ∠OQT = 90°.

WHAT DO WE WANT TO FIND?:
  The length TP.

SOLUTION (method 1 - similar triangles):

  Step 1. Join OT. Let OT intersect PQ at the point R. (Construction.)

  Step 2. From topic 7 (Example 2 consequence / Theorem 10.2 Remark 2), we know that OT bisects ∠PTQ, and because ∆TPQ is isosceles (TP = TQ) with apex at T, the bisector of the apex angle is also perpendicular to PQ and bisects PQ. So OT ⊥ PQ and PR = RQ = 4 cm.

  Step 3. In the right triangle OPR (right-angled at R),
            OR = √(OP² − PR²) = √(5² − 4²) cm = √(25 − 16) cm = √9 cm = 3 cm.

  Step 4. In the right triangle TPR (right-angled at R), we have
            ∠TPR + ∠RPO = 90° = ∠TPR + ∠PTR    (Why? Both sums equal 90°: the first because ∠OPT = 90°, the second because angles in right ∆TPR at R and at P and at T sum to 180°.)
          So ∠RPO = ∠PTR.

  Step 5. Right triangle TRP and right triangle PRO both have a right angle at R, and they share the equal angle ∠PTR = ∠RPO from Step 4. By AA similarity,
            ∆TRP ∼ ∆PRO.

  Step 6. Corresponding sides of similar triangles are in proportion:
            TP / PO = RP / RO
          i.e., TP / 5 = 4 / 3
          so TP = 20 / 3 cm.

SOLUTION (method 2 - Pythagoras):

  Step 1. Let TP = x and TR = y.

  Step 2. Applying the Pythagoras Theorem in right ∆PRT:
            x² = y² + 16    … (1)

  Step 3. Applying the Pythagoras Theorem in right ∆OPT (right-angled at P, with OT = OR + RT = 3 + y):
            x² + 5² = (y + 3)²    … (2)

  Step 4. Subtracting (1) from (2):
            25 = 6y − 7
          so 6y = 32, giving y = 32/6 = 16/3.

  Step 5. Substituting back into (1):
            x² = (16/3)² + 16 = 16(16/9 + 1) = 16 · (16 + 9)/9 = 16 · 25 / 9.
          Therefore x = √(16 · 25 / 9) = 4 · 5 / 3 = 20 / 3.

Both methods give the same answer: TP = 20/3 cm.

WHY THIS STEP? Why does Method 1 introduce a similarity argument when Method 2 just uses Pythagoras twice? Because similarity exposes the ratio TP / PO = RP / RO directly, avoiding the need to solve a system of two equations. Method 2 is more mechanical; Method 1 is more insightful. Both are valid - choose based on which is quicker for the numbers you have.

ERROR ALERT: A student sometimes tries to apply the Pythagoras Theorem to ∆OPT WITHOUT realising it is right-angled at P (not at T). The right angle in ∆OPT is at the point of contact P, because OP is a radius perpendicular to the tangent TP there. Mis-locating the right angle is the most common error in problems of this type - always mark the right angle on the figure before applying Pythagoras.

HOOK: Exercise 10.1 is a short set of four questions that check the very basics from Section 10.2: what a tangent is, how many tangents exist, and the tangent-radius perpendicularity at work. Let us walk through how to approach each question before you attempt them yourself.

RECALL: From Part A we know three essential facts: (1) a circle and a line can share 0, 1, or 2 points (topic 1); (2) the unique line sharing exactly one point with a circle is a tangent, with point of contact (topic 2); and (3) the tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact - Theorem 10.1 (topic 3). All four questions in Exercise 10.1 are answered using only these three ideas.

STRATEGY WALK-THROUGH:

  Q1 (‘How many tangents can a circle have?’) asks you to count the tangents at ALL points of a circle, not from a single outside point. At every point of the circle there is exactly one tangent - and a circle has infinitely many points - so the answer is infinite.

  Q2 (fill-in-the-blanks) tests four definitions from topic 1 and topic 2:
    (i) A tangent meets the circle in one point.
    (ii) A line through two points of a circle is a secant.
    (iii) A circle can have at most two parallel tangents (recall Activity 2 - the two limiting parallel lines on either side of a given secant).
    (iv) The shared point is called the point of contact.
  Each blank is a straight recall from Part A definitions. If you are unsure, re-read topic 2 once.

  Q3 (PQ tangent of radius 5 cm, OQ = 12 cm, find PQ) is the first real computation. Here is the key insight: OP is the radius at P, PQ is the tangent at P, so by Theorem 10.1, ∠OPQ = 90°. Triangle OPQ is right-angled at P, with OP = 5 cm and hypotenuse OQ = 12 cm. By the Pythagoras Theorem,
            PQ² = OQ² − OP² = 144 − 25 = 119
          PQ = √119 cm.
  So option (D) is correct. Watch out: a common wrong answer is 13 cm (option B) from adding squares instead of subtracting, and 12 cm (option A) from just reading OQ.

  Q4 (draw a circle and two parallel lines, one tangent and one secant to the given line) is a construction-style question. Draw a circle. Pick any line ‘L’ in the plane. Draw a line parallel to L that cuts the circle at two points (a secant), and another parallel to L that touches the circle at exactly one point (a tangent). Recall Activity 2: sliding parallel lines across a secant produces a tangent as the limit.

ERROR ALERT: A frequent mistake in Q3 is to forget that the right angle is at P, not at Q. The tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact - that point is P. So the hypotenuse of the right triangle is OQ, not PQ.

CHECK: Attempt Q1-Q4 in your notebook. For Q3, confirm your answer by re-checking which side is the hypotenuse; for Q4, verify by measuring that your chosen tangent line shares exactly one point with the circle.

HOOK: Exercise 10.2 is the main drill of the chapter. It splits naturally into two kinds of questions: computation (find a length / radius / angle) and proof (prove a geometric relation). This topic covers the computation group - Q1, Q2, Q3, Q6, Q7, and Q12. The proof group lives in the next topic.

RECALL: From Part B we have two powerful tools for computation: Theorem 10.1 (tangent ⊥ radius) and Theorem 10.2 (the two tangents from an external point are equal in length). Whenever a tangent meets a radius we get a right angle; whenever two tangents meet an outside point we get two equal segments. Almost every computation in this exercise reduces to one or both of these facts plus the Pythagoras Theorem or an isosceles-triangle angle chase.

STRATEGY WALK-THROUGH:

  Q1 (tangent length 24 cm, OQ = 25 cm, find radius). Set up: the tangent meets the radius at a right angle, so ∆OPQ is right-angled at the point of contact P, with hypotenuse OQ = 25, tangent PQ = 24, and the radius OP unknown. Pythagoras:
            OP² = 25² − 24² = 625 − 576 = 49
          OP = 7 cm. Answer: (A) 7 cm.

  Q2 (TP and TQ are tangents, ∠POQ = 110°, find ∠PTQ). In quadrilateral OPTQ, ∠OPT = ∠OQT = 90° (Theorem 10.1) and ∠POQ = 110° (given). Angle sum of any quadrilateral is 360°:
            ∠PTQ = 360° − 90° − 90° − 110° = 70°. Answer: (B) 70°.

  Q3 (tangents PA, PB inclined at 80°, find ∠POA). The angle ∠APB = 80° is the tangent-tangent angle at the external point P. As in Q2, the quadrilateral OAPB has two right angles at A and B. So
            ∠AOB = 360° − 90° − 90° − 80° = 100°.
          OP bisects ∠AOB (from Theorem 10.2 Remark 2, OP is the angle bisector of ∠APB, and by congruent triangles ∆OAP ≅ ∆OBP, OP also bisects ∠AOB). So
            ∠POA = ½ · 100° = 50°. Answer: (A) 50°.

  Q6 (tangent from A of length 4 cm, OA = 5 cm, find radius). Exactly the same structure as Q1, with different numbers. ∆OPA is right-angled at P with PA = 4, OA = 5. Radius = √(25 − 16) = √9 = 3 cm.

  Q7 (concentric circles, outer radius 5 cm, inner radius 3 cm; find the length of the chord of the outer circle that touches the inner). This is exactly the set-up of Example 1 (topic 6). The chord is tangent to the inner circle at its midpoint, so half-chord = √(5² − 3²) = √16 = 4 cm. Full chord = 8 cm.

  Q12 (triangle ABC circumscribes a circle of radius 4 cm; BD = 8, DC = 6 where D is the contact point on BC; find AB and AC). Use the two-tangents-from-an-external-point theorem three times:
    • Tangents from B to the incircle are BD and BF (where F is the contact on AB): BD = BF = 8 cm.
    • Tangents from C are CD and CE (contact on AC): CD = CE = 6 cm.
    • Tangents from A are AE and AF, both equal to some length x.
  So AB = AF + BF = x + 8, and AC = AE + CE = x + 6. Also BC = BD + DC = 14. Compute the area of ∆ABC two ways: using Heron's formula on sides (x + 8), (x + 6), 14; and using (r × semi-perimeter) with r = 4. Equating the two gives x = 7. Therefore AB = 15 cm and AC = 13 cm.

STRATEGY INSIGHT - choosing the right technique:

  (a) If the problem gives two lengths in a right triangle and asks for the third, use Pythagoras directly (Q1, Q6, Q7 half-chord).

  (b) If the problem gives an angle at an external point or at the centre and asks for the other, use the quadrilateral-angle-sum trick with the two right angles (Q2, Q3).

  (c) If the problem involves multiple tangents from multiple external points (a polygon circumscribing a circle), label every pair of equal tangents from a common external point and solve the resulting system (Q12).

ERROR ALERT: In Q2 and Q3, students often try to use a triangle angle-sum instead of the quadrilateral angle-sum. That fails because there is no triangle that contains both right angles and the given angle directly; the right angles are at different vertices. Always draw the quadrilateral OATB (or OAPB) and sum its four angles to 360°.

HOOK: The second half of Exercise 10.2 is proof-focused: seven questions that ask you to prove a geometric relation rather than compute a value. These consolidate everything in the chapter - Theorem 10.1 perpendicularity, Theorem 10.2 tangent-length equality, and the triangle-congruence criteria you already know.

RECALL: Tools in hand: Theorem 10.1 (tangent ⊥ radius), Theorem 10.2 (equal tangent lengths from an external point), the angle-bisector remark (OP bisects ∠QPR), RHS / SAS / ASA / AAS congruence, and basic angle-sum facts for triangles and quadrilaterals.

STRATEGY WALK-THROUGH:

  Q4 (tangents at the ends of a diameter are parallel). Let AB be a diameter, and let l and m be tangents at A and at B. By Theorem 10.1, OA ⊥ l and OB ⊥ m. But OA and OB lie along the same straight line (since AB is a diameter through the centre O). So l and m are both perpendicular to the same line, hence parallel to each other.

  Q5 (the perpendicular at the point of contact to the tangent passes through the centre). This is essentially the converse of Theorem 10.1. Let the tangent at P be l. Drop a perpendicular to l at P; call this line n. We must show O lies on n. By Theorem 10.1, OP is already perpendicular to l. But through a given point P there is exactly one line perpendicular to l, so n must coincide with the line OP. Hence n passes through O.

  Q8 (quadrilateral ABCD circumscribes a circle: prove AB + CD = AD + BC). Label the four contact points on AB, BC, CD, DA as P, Q, R, S respectively. By Theorem 10.2, tangents from each vertex are equal:
            AP = AS,  BP = BQ,  CQ = CR,  DR = DS.
          Then AB + CD = (AP + PB) + (CR + RD) = AP + BQ + CQ + DS,
          and AD + BC = (AS + SD) + (BQ + QC) = AP + DS + BQ + CQ.
          Both sums are equal. This is the classic ‘Pitot theorem’ for tangential quadrilaterals.

  Q9 (two parallel tangents XY and X′Y′, plus a third tangent AB touching at C, intersecting the first two at A and B: prove ∠AOB = 90°). By Theorem 10.2, the tangents from A (to the circle on the two sides) are equal, so OA bisects the angle between XY and AB at A. Similarly OB bisects the angle between X′Y′ and AB at B. The angles between the two parallel tangents XY and X′Y′ and the transversal AB sum to 180° (co-interior angles), so their halves sum to 90°. Those halves are exactly ∠OAB and ∠OBA. In ∆OAB, ∠AOB = 180° − (∠OAB + ∠OBA) = 180° − 90° = 90°.

  Q10 (angle between two tangents from an external point is supplementary to the angle subtended by the chord of contact at the centre). Let the external point be T, the contact points P, Q. Quadrilateral OPTQ has ∠OPT = ∠OQT = 90°. Angle sum 360° gives ∠PTQ + ∠POQ = 180° - the two angles are supplementary. (Notice how Q2 of the previous topic is just a numerical instance of this proof.)

  Q11 (parallelogram circumscribing a circle is a rhombus). In a parallelogram ABCD, opposite sides are equal: AB = CD, AD = BC. From Q8, AB + CD = AD + BC. Substituting, 2 AB = 2 AD, so AB = AD. A parallelogram with two adjacent sides equal has all sides equal - a rhombus.

  Q13 (opposite sides of a tangential quadrilateral subtend supplementary angles at the centre). Let the contact points on AB, BC, CD, DA be P, Q, R, S. Join O to each contact point and to each vertex. The angle ∠AOB at the centre is the sum of ∠AOP + ∠POB; by the equal-tangent property and RHS congruence, ∠AOP = ∠AOS and ∠POB = ∠BOQ. Summing ∠AOB + ∠COD symmetrically and comparing with ∠BOC + ∠DOA, one finds ∠AOB + ∠COD = ∠BOC + ∠DOA = 180°.

STRATEGY INSIGHT: Every proof in this set ultimately reduces to ONE of three patterns:
  (i) Perpendicularity at the contact point (Q4, Q5).
  (ii) Equal-tangent segments from a common external point, chained around a polygon (Q8, Q11, Q13).
  (iii) Quadrilateral OPTQ with two right angles, 360° angle-sum (Q10 - and Q9 via bisectors).
  Recognising which pattern fits a question is half the work.

ERROR ALERT: A frequent trap is to assume that ‘circumscribes a circle’ means something different from ‘inscribed circle’. They are the same geometric configuration described from two ends: the polygon circumscribes (surrounds) the circle, and the circle is inscribed (drawn inside) the polygon. Both mean the circle touches every side of the polygon.

Given: circle with centre O, diameter AB; tangents l at A and m at B.
To prove: l ∥ m.
Step 1: By Theorem 10.1, OA ⊥ l (the tangent at A is perpendicular to the radius OA).
Step 2: By Theorem 10.1, OB ⊥ m (the tangent at B is perpendicular to the radius OB).
Step 3: Since AB is a diameter, the points A, O, B are collinear; hence OA and OB lie along the same straight line - the line AB.
Step 4: Both l and m are perpendicular to the same straight line AB. Two lines perpendicular to the same line are parallel.
Conclusion: l ∥ m.

recall_questions.answer:
Given: quadrilateral ABCD circumscribes a circle; points of contact P on AB, Q on BC, R on CD, S on DA.
To prove: AB + CD = AD + BC.
Step 1 (Apply Theorem 10.2 at each vertex): Tangents from A give AP = AS. From B: BP = BQ. From C: CQ = CR. From D: DR = DS.
Step 2 (Expand AB + CD): AB + CD = (AP + PB) + (CR + RD) = AP + BP + CQ + DR = AP + BQ + CQ + DR. 
Step 3 (Expand AD + BC): AD + BC = (AS + SD) + (BQ + QC) = AS + DS + BQ + CQ = AP + DR + BQ + CQ.
Step 4 (Compare): Both expansions equal AP + BQ + CQ + DR.
Conclusion: AB + CD = AD + BC.
